svg.title: claudia composes — how text flows around a floating object (proposal)
svg.desc: Four wrap modes on the same paragraph: over the text, around the object, above and below, behind the text; the Wrap Text popover; the rules that make screen and print agree; the mapping to DOCX and ODF; and the open points.
svg.text: claudia composes — text flowing around a floating object

Proposal, nothing of this is built. Today an object floats over the words and nothing wraps (D179). Content is invented. The decision that shapes everything else is who lays the lines out: see the architecture sheet.
A · Four ways, on the same paragraph

The default stays what it is today, so no existing document changes. The wrap belongs to the object's place in the text, not to the picture: the same picture can be over the words in one text and around in another.
1 · Over the text
today, the default
· Lines run full width underneath.
· The object is opaque and hides what it covers.
· Nothing moves when the object does.
2 · Around the object
the lines make room
· Lines shorten to the object's box plus a distance.
· A side narrower than 3 em stays empty.
· Text resumes in full width below it.
3 · Above and below
no text beside it
· Lines stop above the box and go on under it.
· The object stands alone on its lines.
· Good for a figure with a caption.
4 · Behind the text
a watermark, a stamp
· Drawn under the words, which stay readable.
· Lines run full width over it.
· Reached by Tab, not by a click (open point 2).
distance
B · Setting it: Format ▸ Wrap Text…
One entry with one key (Ctrl+Alt+L), and in the object's context menu. It opens next to the held object,
as Rotate By… does; the four tiles are a radio group, the arrow keys move, Enter keeps.
Distance applies to Around and Above and below; the tiles say what each does without jargon.
C · The rules, so that screen and print agree
Each line asks one question: how wide am I here? The answer comes from the objects that reach its band.
box + distance = the band; a line takes
the widest free stretch(es) of its own band
The object's place comes first, from the layout
without this object's wrap: the character's line, plus
dx and dy. So an object never moves the line it hangs
from, and no loop is possible.
Objects are taken in the order of the text. An object
only changes lines at and after its top; the lines
above it stay as they were.
A line's available width is its column minus every
band that reaches it. A stretch narrower than 3 em is
not used, so no single word is stranded beside an
object.
An object keeps to its page: if it will not fit above
the bottom margin it is moved up (D907), and its wrap
applies on that page only.
The same arithmetic runs in the layout library for the
page view and print, and in a test that compares the
lines the editor shows (open point 1).
D · What Word and LibreOffice call them
Import and export, so that wrap survives the round trip.
Claudia
DOCX (wp:anchor)
ODF (style:wrap)
over the text
wrapNone
run-through, foreground
around
wrapSquare + dist*
parallel + fo:margin
above and below
wrapTopAndBottom
none
behind the text
wrapNone, behindDoc
run-through, background
Not modelled: tight and through (a contour round the picture),
in line with the text. They come in as the nearest of the four,
and the original is kept untouched and written back on export,
so a document passing through Claudia does not lose it.
ODF values are from memory of what LibreOffice writes: check
against a file it wrote before any import code (as with rotation).
Open points, each with a recommendation
1 Who lays the lines out
The editor's lines are the browser's (contenteditable), print's are the
engine's. Recommended: the page view and print use the engine, exactly; the flow
view uses the same rules as CSS floats, and a test compares which lines get
narrowed. Details on the architecture sheet.
2 Selecting a Behind object
The layer above the text takes a click, so an object behind the words cannot be
hit without stealing the caret. Recommended: Tab and Edit ▸ Select Next Object
reach it, and so does a click on its visible edge; a click in the words always
places the caret.
3 Four modes, not Word's seven
Tight and through need a contour and 'in line' makes the object a character.
Recommended: four now, imported ones keep their original; 'in line' later as an
anchor kind of its own.
4 One key or four
Every menu entry has a key. Recommended: one entry, Wrap Text… (Ctrl+Alt+L, free
in all three manifests); the four modes are a radio group inside it. Four
entries would need keys on digits, which German AltGr uses.
5 Where the wrap is kept
In the anchor, next to dx and dy (D1023): it is composes-only, and Move already
replaces the whole anchor. Recommended, with a new method set_wrap so that the
history says 'Wrap text around Picture 1'.
6 Default for a new object
Over the text, as today. Recommended for pictures from Edit ▸ Image…: Above and
below, since a picture dropped between two lines rarely wants words over it. The
owner's call.
